title: Embodied mind: conceptual map
content_html:
Embodied mind: conceptual map

Mind = brain–body–world loop
Meaning is enacted in action
Sensorimotor grounding
Predictive processing
Distributed representations
Memory as reconstruction

Embodiment ties together cognitive science (sensorimotor grounding), philosophy (phenomenology/enactivism), neuroscience (perception–action loops), and Buddhism (dependent origination), centring the brain–body–world coupling.

Claim Implication Example
Concepts are sensorimotor-grounded Abstract thought reuses bodily circuits “Grasp an idea” recruits grasping networks
Mind is enacted in activity Meaning emerges in doing, not just representing Gesture improves problem-solving & recall
Self is relational and processual No fixed essence; trainable via practice Meditation reshapes attention & emotion
Memory is reconstructive Recall depends on body state & context Posture/mood shift what is remembered

The embodied mind reframes cognition as situated, enacted, and trainable. It bridges scientific models with contemplative practice by treating experience as emerging from brain–body–world dynamics.

References

  • Lakoff, G., & Johnson, M. (1999). Philosophy in the Flesh: The Embodied Mind and Its Challenge to Western Thought. Basic Books.
  • Merleau‑Ponty, M. (1962). Phenomenology of Perception. Routledge.
  • Thompson, E. (2007). Mind in Life: Biology, Phenomenology, and the Sciences of Mind. Harvard University Press.
  • Varela, F. J., Thompson, E., & Rosch, E. (1991). The Embodied Mind: Cognitive Science and Human Experience. MIT Press.
